name: Bhutan
tagline: Dzongs, high valleys and a fee per night
meta_description: Plan Bhutan on a fair budget: SDF for Indians and international visitors, permits, guides, the road from Siliguri, Paro flights, months and costs.
summary: Bhutan is a Himalayan kingdom you visit with a licensed guide, paying a Sustainable Development Fee per night: ₹1,200 for Indians and US$100 for most others as of 2026. Enter by road at Phuentsholing or fly to Paro, base yourself in Thimphu, Paro and Punakha, and go March–May or September–November.
intro: Bhutan begins a short walk from the Indian town of Jaigaon, through a painted gate into Phuentsholing. From there the road climbs 165 km to Thimphu, the capital, at 2,320 m, and on into a country of steep valleys, rivers, forest and dzongs, the great fortress-monasteries that still serve as district offices and monk bodies. Most first trips cover the western valleys: Thimphu, Paro with the Tiger's Nest, and Punakha with its dzong at the meeting of two rivers. Longer trips go on to Haa, Phobjikha for the black-necked cranes, Trongsa and the old temples of Bumthang.

Bhutan does tourism its own way. Instead of a cheap visa and mass travel, it charges a Sustainable Development Fee, or SDF, for every night you spend in the country. As of 2026, Indian nationals pay ₹1,200 per person per night, and most international visitors pay US$100, a reduced rate from the standard US$200 that runs to 31 August 2027. A licensed guide is required beyond the first checkpoint for everyone. These rules change, so check current status before you travel.

This makes Bhutan more expensive than the Darjeeling or Sikkim hills, but it does not have to be a luxury trip. Indian families can travel by train and bus to the border, stay in certified 3-star hotels and farmhouses, eat local set meals and share a car and guide, and keep a 6-night trip in reach of a mid-range budget. International visitors save by travelling as a group, staying in good 3-star hotels and keeping the route tight, because every extra night adds SDF.

We send people to Bhutan for the dzongs and festivals, for walks to cliffside temples, for farmhouse dinners of red rice and ema datshi, and for the feeling of a country that has kept its dress, architecture and pace of life on its own terms. Plan the route before the length, travel in spring or autumn, book through a licensed operator, and leave time for the slow days: those are what people remember.

story.title: The Zhabdrung, the dzongs and the kings
paras: Modern Bhutan begins with a lama crossing the mountains. In 1616 Ngawang Namgyal, a senior lama of the Drukpa Kagyu school, left Ralung in Tibet after a dispute over who was the true reincarnation of his school's head, and came south into the valleys of western Bhutan. Known as the Zhabdrung, 'at whose feet one submits', he spent the next three decades bringing the valleys under one authority, fighting off Tibetan invasions and rival schools, and building the dzongs. Simtokha, near Thimphu, was the first, in 1629; Punakha followed in 1637–38.

The Zhabdrung set up a dual system of government, with a religious head, the Je Khenpo, and a civil head, the Druk Desi, and gave the country its legal code. The dzong, half fortress, half monastery, half administration, became the shape of the state. After his death in 1651, which was kept secret for decades, power slowly passed to regional governors, the Penlops of Paro and Trongsa, and the 19th century saw long civil wars between them.

The Penlop of Trongsa, Ugyen Wangchuck, came out on top, and on 17 December 1907, at Punakha, he was chosen as the first hereditary king. That date is now Bhutan's National Day. His adviser, Ugyen Dorji, ran Bhutan's dealings with British India from Bhutan House in Kalimpong, a link our hills still remember. A century later the fourth king guided the country to a written constitution, and in 2008 Bhutan held its first national elections and became a constitutional monarchy.
story.source: Ngawang Namgyal, History of Bhutan, Ugyen Wangchuck and Constitution of Bhutan articles (Wikipedia); Karma Phuntsho, The History of Bhutan (2013); Michael Aris, The Raven Crown (1994)

did_you_know: Bhutan allowed television and the internet only in 1999.
Bhutan's 2008 constitution requires that at least 60% of the country remain under forest cover for all time.
The Bhutanese ngultrum is pegged at par to the Indian rupee, and rupees are widely accepted in Bhutan.
In 1994 Bhutan banned climbing peaks above 6,000 m, one reason Gangkhar Puensum, at about 7,570 m, is often called the highest unclimbed mountain in the world.
Bhutan's National Day, 17 December, marks the day in 1907 when Ugyen Wangchuck became the first king at Punakha.

Dzongkha, English, Nepali (Lhotshamkha), Hindi widely understood

highlights.title: The dzongs
highlights.text: Punakha Dzong at the meeting of two rivers, Trongsa Dzong stepped down its ridge, Rinpung Dzong in Paro and the rebuilt Wangdue Phodrang Dzong. These are working buildings, holding district offices and monks, so you see the country's administration and religion in the same courtyards.

highlights.title: The Tiger's Nest hike
highlights.text: Paro Taktsang clings to a cliff about 900 m above the Paro valley floor. The steady 4–6 hour round trip from the car park, with tea at the cafeteria halfway, is the walk almost every visitor does, and it is worth the effort.

highlights.title: Tshechu festivals
highlights.text: Masked dances in dzong courtyards, families in their best gho and kira, and a giant thangka unrolled at dawn. Paro in spring and Thimphu in autumn are the best known; Punakha, Wangdue and Bumthang hold smaller ones with fewer tour groups.

highlights.title: Phobjikha and the cranes
highlights.text: From late October to February, black-necked cranes winter in the broad glacial valley of Phobjikha at about 2,900–3,000 m. Watch them at dawn, walk the Gangtey Nature Trail, and sleep in a farmhouse with a hot stone bath.

highlights.title: High passes and walks
highlights.text: Dochula with its 108 chortens, Chele La at about 3,988 m on the road to Haa, Pele La and Yotong La on the way east. For walkers, the Druk Path Trek links Paro and Thimphu over 4–6 days past high lakes.

highlights.title: Farmhouses and food
highlights.text: A night in a registered farmhouse in Paro, Haa or Phobjikha, with red rice, ema datshi, buckwheat dishes and butter tea, often costs less than a hotel and gives you the best food and conversation of the trip.

getting_there: From the Darjeeling hills and Siliguri, the cheapest way in is by road. Buses and shared vehicles run from Siliguri to Jaigaon, about 155–170 km and 4–6 hours through the Dooars, or take a train from NJP to Hasimara and a taxi for the last 18 km. Walk through the gate into Phuentsholing, complete your permit formalities, meet your guide and drive 165 km, 5–6 hours, up to Thimphu. By air, Drukair and Bhutan Airlines fly into Paro from Delhi, Kolkata and, on some days, Bagdogra, as well as from Kathmandu, Bangkok, Singapore and other hubs. Paro flights depend on visibility, so keep buffer time on both ends. Smaller land crossings at Gelephu and Samdrup Jongkhar serve central and eastern Bhutan. Routes, schedules and fares change; check current status before you travel.
permits: Indian nationals need a valid passport or Voter ID card to get a free Entry Permit, online or at Phuentsholing or Paro, which covers Thimphu and Paro. Route permits for Punakha, Haa, Phobjikha, Trongsa, Bumthang, Gasa and beyond are issued in Thimphu on working days; your operator arranges them. Other nationalities apply for a visa, US$40, through a licensed operator or the online system before travel. Everyone pays the SDF per night and must have a licensed guide beyond the first checkpoint; treks need a licensed trekking guide. Check current status before you travel.

budget.summary: Bhutan's costs come in four parts: the SDF per night, the licensed guide, the vehicle, and your hotels and meals. You cannot avoid the first two, so save on the rest. Travel overland from Siliguri instead of flying, share one car and guide among four to six people, stay in certified 3-star hotels and farmhouses, eat set meals where drivers and guides eat, and keep the route tight so you are not paying SDF for nights spent in the car.
costs: ₹1,200 per person per night; children 6–12 half, under 6 free
US$100 per person per night to 31 Aug 2027, plus US$40 visa
tips: Travel in a group of four to six, because the car and guide cost the same per day for two people or six.
Enter overland at Phuentsholing instead of flying to Paro; the bus or train from Siliguri costs a fraction of a flight.
Choose March, early April, late November or early December for lower hotel rates than the festival weeks.
Ask every operator whether their quote includes SDF, since some leave it out to look cheaper.
International visitors save US$100 per adult per night by travelling before the reduced SDF rate ends on 31 August 2027, unless it is extended.

months.summary: January is cold and dry, with clear skies and the best mountain views of the year from Dochula and Chele La. Thimphu nights fall below freezing, but Punakha and Wangdue in the lower valleys are mild and pleasant. The black-necked cranes are in Phobjikha. Snow can close Chele La and slow other passes, so keep a spare day. Gasa's hot springs are at their busiest with Bhutanese families.
months.tip: Base yourself in Punakha, which is 10 °C warmer than Thimphu, and make day trips up to the passes.
months.price_note: Low season: many hotels offer lower rates and festival-week crowds are absent.

months.weather: Thimphu −1–14 °C, mostly dry; warming late in the month
months.summary: February is still cold in Thimphu and Paro but brightening, with clear mornings and the first plum and peach blossom in the lower valleys towards the end of the month. The Punakha Drubchen and Tshechu may fall in February or March, depending on the lunar calendar. Cranes are still in Phobjikha until about the end of the month. Losar, the Bhutanese new year, often falls in February.
months.tip: Check the lunar calendar early; the Punakha festival dates fix whether February or March is better.
months.price_note: Still off-season rates in most places, except Punakha during its festival.

months.summary: March is when spring arrives: rhododendrons start to flower on the passes, magnolia and peach blossom appear in the valleys, and days are comfortable for walking. The Paro Tshechu often falls in late March or April, and the Punakha festival may still be on early in the month. Mountain views are good but hazier than in winter. It is a fine month for Tiger's Nest and Punakha.
months.tip: Book Paro hotels months ahead if your dates overlap the Paro Tshechu.
months.price_note: Rates rise from mid-March, sharply in Paro during the festival week.

months.summary: April is one of the best months: warm days, flowering rhododendrons along Dochula and Chele La, and good trekking weather. The Paro Tshechu often falls in early April. It is a good time to start the Druk Path Trek or visit Haa. Haze can hide the high peaks by midday, so go up to the passes early. Hotels are busy, especially around the festival.
months.tip: Start passes and hikes early; afternoon cloud is common from April.
months.price_note: Peak season: expect full rates and book certified hotels well ahead.

months.summary: May is warm and green, with rhododendrons still flowering higher up and comfortable temperatures in Bumthang and Haa. Pre-monsoon showers start towards the end of the month. It is a good time for central Bhutan and for walks on Chele La. Indian school holidays bring more families from mid-May, so book early. Lower valleys like Punakha start to get hot.
months.tip: Spend more nights high, in Haa, Bumthang or Phobjikha, and fewer in hot Punakha.
months.price_note: Busy with Indian summer holidays from mid-May; book hotels and cars early.

months.weather: Thimphu 15–25 °C, monsoon begins, rain most afternoons
months.summary: The monsoon arrives in June, bringing rain, cloud and the first landslides on the Phuentsholing–Thimphu highway. Mornings can still be clear, the valleys are green and there are far fewer tourists. Mountain views are rare. It is a reasonable month for a short Thimphu–Paro trip with flexible plans, but not for treks or long road journeys east.
months.tip: Keep the route short and fly in or out of Paro if road delays would break your plans.
months.price_note: Rates start to fall; ask operators about monsoon discounts on hotels.

months.weather: Thimphu 15–25 °C, heavy rain, cloud and fog
months.summary: July is the heart of the monsoon, with heavy rain, leeches on forest trails and landslides that can close roads for hours. Views are mostly hidden. Still, the valleys are at their greenest, the Haa Summer Festival celebrates the valley's herding and farming life, and you will have sights to yourself. Only come with flexible dates and patience.
months.tip: Build at least one spare day into any road journey and avoid long drives east.
months.price_note: Lowest demand of the year; good hotel deals but SDF and guide costs stay the same.

months.summary: August is wet, with the same monsoon conditions as July: frequent rain, low cloud and landslide risk on most roads, especially the highway up from Phuentsholing. Flights into Paro can be delayed by cloud. If you must travel, stick to Thimphu and Paro, keep plans flexible and enjoy the empty dzongs. Late August sometimes brings clearer breaks.
months.tip: Fly into Paro rather than driving from Phuentsholing if your dates are fixed.
months.price_note: Off-season rates continue; operators are more willing to negotiate.

months.weather: Thimphu 14–23 °C, rain easing, clearer by late month
months.summary: September starts wet and clears as the monsoon withdraws, with fresh, green valleys and rice ripening in Punakha and Wangdue. The Thimphu Tshechu often falls in late September or October, and hotels fill fast for it. Late September is a good time to begin an autumn trip before the October peak. Some landslide risk remains early in the month.
months.tip: Aim for the second half of the month, when roads are drier and rice terraces are golden.
months.price_note: Rates climb from mid-month, peaking around the Thimphu Tshechu.

months.summary: October is the best month for weather: clear skies, crisp air and long views of the snow peaks from the passes. The Thimphu Tshechu often falls now, and Jambay Lhakhang Drup in Bumthang may begin late in the month. It is also the busiest month, with Puja holiday travellers from India and international groups. Book hotels, cars and flights months ahead.
months.tip: Book three to six months ahead for October, especially if your dates include a festival or the Puja holidays.
months.price_note: Peak season: full rates everywhere and few last-minute deals.

months.summary: November is clear, dry and a little colder, with excellent views and fewer crowds than October. The black-necked cranes arrive in Phobjikha, and the Black-necked Crane Festival is held there around 11 November. Jambay Lhakhang Drup in Bumthang often falls this month. It is a fine time for the Druk Path Trek and for the long drive east via Trongsa.
months.tip: Book Phobjikha early for the crane festival around 11 November; rooms in the valley are limited.
months.price_note: Busy early in the month; rates and crowds ease after mid-November.

months.weather: Thimphu −2–13 °C, dry, clear; snow possible on passes
months.summary: December is cold, dry and clear, with some of the best mountain views of the year and quiet dzongs. Cranes are in Phobjikha, Punakha's lower valley is pleasant, and Gasa's hot springs fill with Bhutanese bathers. National Day on 17 December brings celebrations. Snow can close Chele La and slow Pele La and Yotong La, so keep a spare day.
months.tip: Pack proper winter clothes; Thimphu and Paro nights fall below freezing.
months.price_note: Low season apart from Christmas and New Year week, when some hotels raise rates.

faqs.q: Do Indians need a passport to visit Bhutan
faqs.a: No. Indian nationals can use either a valid Indian passport or a Voter ID card (EPIC) to get the Entry Permit, online or at Phuentsholing or Paro. Aadhaar and driving licences are not accepted for this. Children need their own valid document, so check with your operator. The Entry Permit is free. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How much is the SDF for Indians in Bhutan
faqs.a: As of 2026, Indian nationals pay a Sustainable Development Fee of ₹1,200 per person per night. Children aged 6 to 12 pay half and those under 6 pay nothing. A couple on a six-night trip pays ₹14,400 in SDF. Day visitors who stay in the Phuentsholing zone for under 24 hours do not pay it. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How much is the SDF for international visitors
faqs.a: Most international visitors pay US$100 per person per night as of 2026, a reduced rate from the standard US$200 that the Department of Tourism set for 1 September 2023 to 31 August 2027. A US$40 visa fee is added. Children aged 6 to 12 pay half. After August 2027 the rate may return to US$200. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is a guide mandatory in Bhutan for Indians
faqs.a: Yes, under current rules. The Department of Tourism notification of 8 April 2026 restated that a licensed guide is required for tourists beyond the first checkpoint, including Indian visitors. In practice you book through a licensed operator who supplies the guide and a Bhutan-registered car. Treks need a licensed trekking guide. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Bhutan
faqs.a: March to May and September to November. October and November give the clearest skies and mountain views; spring brings rhododendrons and the Paro Tshechu. December to February is cold but dry, with cranes in Phobjikha and lower prices. June to August is the monsoon, with rain, cloud and landslide risk on the roads.

faqs.q: How do I reach Bhutan from Siliguri or NJP
faqs.a: Take a bus from Siliguri to Jaigaon, about 4–6 hours for ₹150–300, or a train from NJP to Hasimara and a taxi for the last 18 km. Walk through the gate into Phuentsholing, complete your Entry Permit, meet your guide and drive about 165 km, 5–6 hours, to Thimphu. A reserved car from Siliguri to Jaigaon costs about ₹4,500–6,000, indicative 2026.

faqs.q: How many days are enough for Bhutan
faqs.a: Five to six nights covers Thimphu, Paro and Punakha comfortably, including the Tiger's Nest hike. Add two nights for Haa or Phobjikha, and three or four more for Trongsa and Bumthang. If you enter by road from Phuentsholing, add a night there to break the journey. Because SDF is charged per night, plan the route first.

faqs.q: What is the cheapest way to visit Bhutan from India
faqs.a: Travel overland from Siliguri, keep to the Thimphu–Paro–Punakha circuit, share a car and guide among four to six people, stay in certified 3-star hotels or farmhouses, and travel outside festival weeks. A budget six-night package for a group of four to six Indians can cost roughly ₹30,000–40,000 per person including SDF, indicative 2026. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I use Indian rupees and UPI in Bhutan
faqs.a: Yes, rupees are widely accepted at par with the ngultrum, but carry ₹500 and smaller notes. Card payments work in many hotels and larger shops, and some places accept UPI-linked payments, though coverage outside towns is patchy. ATMs in Thimphu, Paro and Phuentsholing are reliable; carry cash for smaller places. Check current status before you travel.
